A temperature inversion is a layer where temperature increases with height instead of decreasing. Normally air cools with altitude (~6.5 °C/km), so warm surface air rises and mixes. With an inversion, the warmer air aloft sits over cooler air below — a stable, stratified layer that suppresses vertical mixing. Because the surface air can't rise and disperse, pollutants (smog) accumulate in the shallow layer below the inversion, often capped by it. Common causes: nocturnal radiative cooling, subsidence in high-pressure systems, warm fronts, valleys with cold air drainage. Inversions break when the sun heats the ground or wind mixes the layer.
